questions.explain: DMVs reflect current state since the last restart; they keep no history. A scheduled snapshot (e.g., 5-minute samples of wait stats and query stats) builds the time series you'll need during the next incident review.
options: DMVs are read-only, so snapshots are the only way to query them at all.
DMVs reset on service restart — they are a window into current activity, not history. Snapshots give you the history needed for post-mortems and trend analysis.
Snapshotting DMVs is required for Query Store to work.
DMVs can only be queried by sysadmin, so snapshots make them visible to operators.
questions.q: Why does the chapter recommend snapshotting key DMVs like sys.dm_os_wait_stats into a DBA utility database on a schedule?

questions.explain: sys.dm_exec_requests exposes blocking_session_id, wait_type, and wait_time per request; joining it to sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks builds the full blocking chain from lead blocker down to every waiter.
options: sys.dm_os_wait_stats
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
sys.dm_exec_requests (joined to sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks)
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats
questions.q: In SQL Server, which DMV exposes the blocking chain — including the blocking session id and wait type of blocked sessions?

questions.explain: The chapter's recommended table lists long-running query alerts as warning at > 5 minutes and critical at > 15 minutes, combined with duration-based triggering so transient spikes don't page anyone.
options: Warning at > 1 minute, critical at > 5 minutes
Warning at > 5 minutes, critical at > 15 minutes
Warning at > 15 minutes, critical at > 1 hour
Warning at > 30 seconds, critical at > 2 minutes
questions.q: According to the chapter's alert threshold table, which pair of thresholds is recommended for a long-running query alert?

questions.explain: The chapter's convention: rebuild above 30% fragmentation, reorganize between 10% and 30%, and leave indexes below 10% alone — the basis of an adaptive, idempotent maintenance job.
options: Rebuild indexes above 30% fragmentation, reorganize between 10% and 30%, leave below 10% alone.
Rebuild indexes above 50% fragmentation, reorganize between 30% and 50%, leave below 30% alone.
Reorganize indexes above 30%, rebuild above 60%; anything below 30% needs no action.
Always rebuild every index nightly regardless of fragmentation level.
questions.q: What is the standard fragmentation guidance given for SQL Server index maintenance?

questions.explain: When Query Store fills its storage quota it flips to read-only mode and stops collecting without an obvious alert — you must monitor actual_state_desc to catch it. Also note plan forcing on an AG primary does not replicate forcing to secondaries.
options: Because Query Store automatically deletes plans older than 7 days.
Because when Query Store hits its MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB quota it flips to read-only and silently stops collecting.
Because Query Store only captures data on the primary replica.
Because Query Store plans are encrypted and require a key rotation job.
questions.q: Why must you monitor Query Store's own storage state via sys.database_query_store_options?
